text: Every endpoint that fronts a model — accepting a prompt, running retrieval, triggering an agent — is still an ordinary HTTP API first. That's the mental model to start from. Authentication, authorization, rate limiting, input validation, all of it still applies in full. What's different is a handful of places where an AI endpoint's own behavior, especially its wildly variable compute cost per call, changes how those same fundamentals need to be tuned.

Authentication and input validation don't need reinventing. Every call needs a credential — short-lived tokens or mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic, scoped so a caller permitted to query one model can't reuse that credential against a more sensitive one. Input still gets validated before it reaches the model. And a response is generated text, not a value your own code constructed, so it needs its own exit check before it reaches the caller — that's the part worth sitting with.

Here's the cost problem a traditional rate limit misses entirely. A fixed requests-per-minute limit assumes every request costs about the same to serve. For a model endpoint, a two-sentence prompt and a prompt that pastes in an entire report can differ in compute cost by orders of magnitude, while both still count as exactly one request. An attacker who understands that can run a denial-of-wallet attack: stay under the request-count ceiling while deliberately sending large, expensive requests that run up inference cost far faster than normal traffic would.

The fix is measuring the limit in tokens or estimated cost, not request count. Track input tokens plus expected output tokens per caller over a rolling window, and throttle once that cost budget is exhausted — not just once a request count is. Pair it with a hard per-request input size ceiling on prompt length, retrieved context, and any file upload, enforced at the API layer itself. A larger context window isn't just more expensive; it's also more room for prompt-injection content to hide in.

On the way out, run every response through an output stage before it reaches the caller: scan for disallowed content, validate against an expected schema when the response is meant to be structured, and safely encode any markup the client will render rather than assuming model output is automatically safe to display. A leaked fragment from an upstream access-control bug, or reproduced personal data, can surface in generated text the same way it could in any other response — this is the check that catches it.

An AI endpoint's security comes from applying ordinary API discipline everywhere, tuned for cost-driven rate limits and generated-text output. Next lesson moves from the API boundary into the agent itself — what an LLM with tool-calling access should be allowed to do completely on its own, and where a human approval gate belongs instead.
